transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-06
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Michael Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Laura Martinez (CISO, Edenbridge), Tomokazu Sato (Platform Eng), Nina Patel (Compliance)
---
Auto-summary (auto gen): Discussed audit log coverage (admin vs user events), export formats (S3 / webhook / Kinesis), retention policy scenarios, KMS integration and key custody, legal hold and immutable storage options, next steps to run a scrubbed export into customer's Splunk instance for validation.
Topics: audit capture surface, export options, retention windows and costs, KMS/HSM integration, RBAC/SSO logging, deletion / legal hold
---
[00:00] Michael Chen (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — I see Laura, Tomo, Nina. Hi Priya. We're here to walk through Edenbridge's audit log needs and how Redwood captures admin activity and supports exports/retention.
[00:28] Laura Martinez (CISO): Thanks Michael. High level: we're evaluating whether we can meet our 3rd party audit requirements — SOC2 and ISO — and particularly how admin actions and elevation are captured. Need to know what you log, how long it stays, whether it's tamper-evident, and how we can pull it into our SIEM.
[00:50] Priya Nair (Redwood SE): Great. We'll go through what events are recorded, export paths, retention defaults, and our KMS options. Quick note that some product names in my notes came out a bit off in the automated transcription.
[01:12] Tomokazu Sato (Platform Eng): Also curious about user events vs admin events. We need both, but admin trail with sudo/elevations is the most critical for auditors.
[01:27] Michael Chen: Totally. Quick overview — Redwood captures three broad categories: control-plane admin activity (console/API/role changes, token/key rotations), data-plane inference events (request metadata, non-sensitive request metadata), and system-level infra events (node restarts, autoscale changes). For audits you care most about admin activity and provisioning events.
[01:52] Nina Patel (Compliance): When you say request metadata, do you capture prompts or full conversation content? That's a big no for us unless consented and encrypted differently.
[02:05] Priya Nair: By default we do NOT persist user prompt text in long term audit logs. Production hosted pipeline keeps short-lived telemetry for routing/diagnostics; text payloads are not stored in audit exports unless a customer opts-in and has a private deployment / dedicated contract that allows for controlled storage. We capture identifiers, request IDs, model version, token counts, timestamps, caller identity, and top-level response status and error codes.
[02:40] Laura Martinez: OK that helps. For SOC2, auditors usually want to see immutable admin logs and evidence of key rotations and who approved changes. How does Redwood show immutability?
[02:55] Priya Nair: Two options. In hosted: we offer an append-only audit stream with write-once retention flags for X days, plus signed log entries (HMAC) at ingest to provide tamper evidence. For Private/Dedicated customers you can integrate with your object store with object-lock/immutable S3 bucket configuration or our write-to-SIEM connector so logs land under your custody.
[03:20] Tomokazu Sato: So if we use Private deployment with our S3, we can rely on S3 Object Lock and our KMS?
[03:30] Priya Nair: Yes. In that flow you control the KMS keys; Redwood will call your KMS for envelope encryption or encrypt at-rest under your key. We support AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, and customer HSM via PKCS#11 in the on-prem package.
[03:50] Laura Martinez: What about rotation windows and proof of rotation? Auditors ask for rotation logs.
[03:58] Michael Chen: Rotation events are logged as admin events — who, when, old key id, new key id — and we produce rotation records in the audit export. If you're using customer-managed keys, the key rotation is performed via your KMS and we capture the rotation event and KMS key id.
[04:18] [04:18] Speaker 1 (automated): inaudible
[04:25] Nina Patel: Is the key material ever visible to Redwood? We need to ensure we don't have plaintext key access.
[04:31] Priya Nair: No, Redwood does not unwrap customer KMS keys in hosted mode. For envelope encryption we keep only the encrypted DEK; unwrapping occurs within your KMS. The on-prem package is the only case where key material may be under customer admin control entirely.
[04:49] [05:00] Michael Chen: Let's talk export formats: we support push to S3 (NDJSON or gzipped batches), syslog/Splunk HTTP Event Collector, pub/sub streams (Kinesis / Pub/Sub) and a webhook/HTTP push for real-time admin streams. You can also pull via API with pagination.
[05:22] Tomokazu Sato: For Splunk we prefer HEC with TLS and token auth. Does your export include a canonical schema map?
[05:30] Priya Nair: Yes we have a schema (we'll share the mapping spreadsheet). Typical fields: event_id, timestamp, actor_id, actor_role, event_type (create_user, assign_role, rotate_key, create_api_token, run_backup), resource_id, resource_type, old_value, new_value, request_id, client_ip, region, response_code. We also include a provenance hash for each event.
[05:58] Laura Martinez: Can you show an example event?
[06:02] Priya Nair: Sure — we'll attach a sample NDJSON row in follow-up. It's scrubbed — no PII.
[06:10] [06:10] Michael Chen: About retention — our hosted default retention for audit events is 90 days for high-fidelity logs and 365 days for summary indexes. You can request extended retention for up to 3 years as an add-on. For Dedicated/Private customers retention is per the customer's storage policy.
[06:32] Nina Patel: Our compliance baseline requires 7 years for certain admin actions for some regs — can you support that?
[06:40] Priya Nair: For long-term 7-year retention we recommend either Dedicated with offload to your S3/GCS with object-lock or an archival pipeline that snapshots NDJSON to your cold storage (Glacier/Archive) under your KMS. Hosted can do longer retention but it becomes a contractual add-on and there are cost considerations. We'll include cost estimates.
[07:03] Tomokazu Sato: What about legal hold? If there's an ongoing investigation we may need to freeze deletion for a subset of records.
[07:12] Michael Chen: We support legal hold flags on export sets. If you route to your bucket with object-lock, you can apply retention/hold there. If you use Redwood hosted retention, we have a legal hold API that toggles retention for a given export id; that requires an enterprise support request so there are guardrails.
[07:35] Laura Martinez: Are there controls around who can export logs? We need RBAC for export capabilities.
[07:42] Priya Nair: Yes, export actions are gated by RBAC. Admin roles: LogViewer, LogExporter, SecurityAdmin — each has least privilege by default. Exports require two-step approval if you enable privileged export mode: an approve token from a separate admin who is not the exporter.
[08:05] Nina Patel: How are SSO events (SAML/SCIM provisioning) surfaced? Those are critical for our identity proof.
[08:12] Priya Nair: SSO events are captured: SAML assertion validation failures, SCIM user creation/deprovision, lastLogin timestamps, and changes to SCIM mappings. We include SAML assertion ID and timestamp but not the assertion body.
[08:30] [08:30] Tomokazu Sato: On tamper evidence — you said HMAC. Can we also get ledger-style hashes or a signed chain?
[08:38] Priya Nair: We have an optional signed-chain mode: log entries include prev_hash and entry_hash signed by a rotating signing key; we provide the public key for verification at export time. For the highest assurance we recommend combining with your immutable storage and our signature chain.
[08:58] Michael Chen: Competition note — some vendors only give truncated logs or rely entirely on hosted buffers; our differentiation is flexible export + signature + customer KMS integration.
[09:12] Laura Martinez: Data residency — we need audit logs stored in EU for EU customer records.
[09:18] Michael Chen: We support region-specific export endpoints. You can opt to have audit exports written to region-local object stores. For hosted customers we make region guarantees via contract; for Private/Dedicated you control residency.
[09:33] Nina Patel: Any PII redaction? For example IP addresses or user emails in logs?
[09:40] Priya Nair: We can redact or hash specific fields at export time. By default we keep client_ip but can hash it or remove it on request. We'll show you the per-field redaction controls in the runbook.
[09:58] [10:10] Tomokazu Sato: What about retention costs estimation? Our finance team needs an estimate of storage costs for 7 years of logs at projected volume ~ 30 GB/month.
[10:20] Michael Chen: We'll run numbers: for cold archive vs hot S3, price differs by order of magnitude. We'll include a spreadsheet with examples for 90/365/3yr/7yr.
[10:32] Laura Martinez: On legal/regulatory audit artifacts — beyond raw logs, auditors want a narrative plus proof of process, like who approved changes. Can Redwood produce an audit package?
[10:45] Priya Nair: Yes, we can produce audit packs that include: the NDJSON export for the date range, rotation logs, RBAC configuration snapshot, policy change events, and a signed integrity file. We can also provide a runbook extract that states our retention and deletion workflow.
[11:05] Nina Patel: How granular is the RBAC snapshot? We need role membership and principals at the time of event.
[11:11] Priya Nair: Snapshots include role membership with effective timestamps; we can export a mapping table for any historical timepoint for the time window retained.
[11:23] [11:45] Michael Chen: A couple operational caveats — streaming real-time to SIEM can increase costs due to egress and ingestion. Batching to NDJSON and periodic transfer is more cost efficient and still forensically useful.
[11:58] Tomokazu Sato: Do you support signed S3 uploads with a managed multi-part approach?
[12:04] Priya Nair: Yes signed uploads or server-side push from Redwood. For bigger volumes we recommend multipart with gzip chunking and manifest files.
[12:18] Laura Martinez: How do we prove chain-of-custody for evidence requested by legal later?
[12:24] Priya Nair: Chain-of-custody is supported by a combination of push logs with signed manifests, KMS-backed encryption under your key, and optionally object-lock. We timestamp manifests and include the signer key id which you can cross-verify.
[12:40] [13:00] Michael Chen: Quick Q for customer: who will own the SIEM integration? Tomo, your team or security?
[13:06] Tomokazu Sato: Platform team will do the initial config, security will own validation. We'll take the sample export and test ingestion.
[13:14] Nina Patel: We'll need an internal compliance checklist item with clear owners.
[13:18] Michael Chen: Great — we'll include that in next steps.
[13:25] [20:00] -- fast-forward in transcript, mid-call technical deep dive --
[20:00] Priya Nair: Diving into schema specifics: event_type taxonomy, normalized enum values, and how we represent delta changes. Example: assign_role event will include resource_id (role:security_admin), actor_id, target_principal, grant_scope, effective_from, and audit_metadata. We also include pre/post snapshots when applicable.
[24:40] Tomokazu Sato: Regarding deletion operations — do you log purge actions and who requested them?
[24:48] Priya Nair: Yes. Delete/purge/export actions are logged with requestor, approver if applicable, timestamp, and export retention policy id. There's also an audit trail for scheduled deletions.
[29:10] Laura Martinez: For regulatory proof, can you produce a verification report showing no deletions occurred during a period aside from scheduled ones?
[29:18] Michael Chen: Yes, we can produce a deletion report that enumerates deletion events and reasons and cross-check against legal hold flags.
[33:00] [33:00] Nina Patel: A practical question: if we want to test ingest — can you provide a scrubbed 30-day export?
[33:08] Priya Nair: Yes we'll provide a scrubbed NDJSON of the last 30 days, anonymized, with schema. That's in the action items.
[33:20] Tomokazu Sato: For live testing we'll spin up a test Splunk HEC endpoint and give Redwood a token.
[33:27] Michael Chen: Perfect. We'll coordinate off-line.
[38:00] [38:00] Priya Nair: On KMS details: for envelope encryption we send DEKs encrypted under your KMS key id. We never persist plaintext DEKs; all decryption happens in the enclave or within your HSM boundary for private deployments.
[38:22] Laura Martinez: Do you have attestations for HSM integration?
[38:28] Priya Nair: We have integration docs and examples; for higher assurance we can do a joint security run with our infra team to show the flow. We'll share the integration guide link in the follow-up.
[42:00] [42:00] Michael Chen: About monitoring and alerts — we can hook admin anomalies into Redwood Console and push alerts to PagerDuty or your SIEM. Detection examples: mass role grants, API key creation spikes, or export bursts.
[42:20] Tomokazu Sato: Can alerts be bulk exported? We want an incident timeline alongside the raw logs.
[42:26] Priya Nair: Yes incidents and alerts are included in the export. They include incident_id, timeline events, correlation ids, and references to raw audit events.
[46:00] [46:00] Laura Martinez: Anything we should be aware of for FedRAMP-like requests?
[46:05] Michael Chen: For higher fed controls we recommend Private deployment with in-region VPC, customer-managed KMS, and object-lock archival. We'll surface the controls mapping in the SOC2 pack.
[49:00] [49:00] Nina Patel: On anonymization — we need to be sure no email addresses leak in old admin comments or notes. Are free-text admin notes scrubbed?
[49:08] Priya Nair: Free-text fields are scrubbed on request. Out of box they may contain admin-entered notes; we can set a policy to remove or redact prior to export.
[51:00] [51:00] Michael Chen: Recap — we will: 1) send SOC2/ISO docs, 2) share schema + sample NDJSON, 3) provide retention/cost spreadsheet, 4) deliver scrubbed 30-day export for Splunk ingest test, 5) schedule 30m pilot week of 5/19.
[51:26] Laura Martinez: Sounds good. Also include the legal hold and object-lock options in writing.
[51:32] Michael Chen: Will do. Anything else?
[51:38] Tomokazu Sato: If you can include a quick note on how to verify the signed-chain (sample commands to verify) that would help our auditors.
[51:45] Priya Nair: We'll add that to the runbook — sample openssl verification commands and a small python verifier.
[52:00] [52:00] Nina Patel: Ok that's great. We'll review the artifacts and come back with questions.
[52:08] Michael Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the items and get the sample export ready.
[52:14] [End of call notes]
